core: An array is a fixed-size, contiguous block of memory holding elements, typically of one type, accessed by an integer index
Zero-based indexing and the address formula: the element at index i lives at base_address + i * element_size
Random access by index is O(1): the address is computed with one multiplication and one addition, independent of the array's length
Operation complexities: index/read O(1); search an unsorted array O(n); insert or delete in the middle O(n) because remaining elements must shift
Why the size is fixed: a contiguous block is reserved up front, so growing it in place is not generally possible
supporting: The memory offset formula requires all elements to be the same size, which is why arrays typically hold one element type
A concrete fixed-type array in practice: Python's array module, a C array, or a Java array
Distinction between time cost (shifting) and the fact that the index computation itself is constant work
outOfScope: Dynamic arrays, resizing, append/grow semantics and amortized O(1) append (belongs to the lists topic)
Linked lists and Python's built-in list type as the main subject (lists topic)
Stacks (LIFO) and queues (FIFO) as structures (their own topics)
Sorting and searching algorithms in depth (searching topic)

claims.claim: An array is an assemblage of items randomly accessible by an integer index; arrays typically have a fixed size and use either 0-based or 1-based indexing.
In C, an array is a contiguously allocated nonempty sequence of objects of one element type, with the element count fixed for the array's lifetime.
Arrays offer constant-time O(1) access to any element by index; this is what lets get(i) and set(i,x) run in constant time.
The address of the element at index i in a zero-based array equals base_address + i * element_size; for base 1000 and 4-byte elements, index 3 is at address 1012 (verified by arithmetic in python3).

Adding or removing an element near the middle of an array-backed list means a large number of elements must be shifted; inserting at index k in a length-n array shifts (n - k) elements, so middle insert and delete are O(n) (shift counts verified in python3).
Searching an unsorted array for a value requires linear search, examining elements one by one, which is O(n) in the worst case; NIST notes unordered arrays require linear search.

Python's array module stores an array of basic values (characters, integers, floating-point numbers) whose element type is constrained by a type code chosen at creation, giving a compact representation; this is a true fixed-type array, distinct from Python's general-purpose list.
